title: Coded messages
concept: Text · characters as numbers, and bytes
description: Messages leave the tower as numbers. Shift letters to make a simple code, and count the bytes a message really takes.

tasks.title: Letters are numbers too
tasks.body: A computer stores each character as a number called its code point: ord("a") is 97 and chr(97) is "a". The letters a to z have codes one after another, so moving a letter along the alphabet is adding to its code.
tasks.detail: To send text, its code points are written as bytes using an encoding. UTF-8, the most common one, uses one byte for each plain English letter and more for others: é takes two bytes and many emoji four. So len(text) counts characters, while len(text.encode("utf-8")) counts bytes.

tasks.code:
# Every character is stored as a number
print(ord("A"), ord("a"))
print(chr(98))
print(len("café"))
print(len("café".encode("utf-8")))
tasks.note: Capital A and small a have different codes. "café" has four characters but five bytes, because é takes two in UTF-8.

tasks.question: What does chr(ord("y") + 2) give?
tasks.why: y is 121, and 123 is the character {. To wrap around to a, the code has to come back to the start of the alphabet, which % 26 does.

tasks.prompt: Predict, then run: print ord("z") and chr(ord("z") + 1). Then measure len("🙂".encode("utf-8")).

Write shift(message, steps), which moves every small letter a to z that many places along the alphabet, wrapping round from z to a, and leaves every other character as it is: shift("abc xyz", 2) returns "cde zab". steps can be negative or bigger than 26. Then write byte_count(text), which returns how many bytes text takes in UTF-8. Do not ask for input: the check calls your functions with its own values.
hints: For each character, check whether it is a small letter. If it is, work out its place in the alphabet, 0 for a to 25 for z, with ord(ch) - ord("a").
Add steps to the place, and % 26 keeps it from 0 to 25, even for negative steps. chr() of the place plus ord("a") gives the new letter. encode("utf-8") turns text into bytes for byte_count().
With other names, for digits: chr((ord(d) - ord("0") + 1) % 10 + ord("0")) moves a digit one along, wrapping 9 round to 0.

error_hints.text: Use the parameter names from each def line, spelled the same way.
ord() takes one character and chr() one number. Build the new message by joining characters.
shift("abc xyz", 2) should return "cde zab": z wraps round to b, and the space stays a space.
shift("hello", -1) should return "gdkkn": negative steps go back along the alphabet.
byte_count("café") should return 5: é takes two bytes in UTF-8.
Check a shift bigger than 26: it wraps round more than once.
Check capital letters, digits and marks: they stay as they are.

similar_example.note: Digits moved along their own ten codes, wrapping round. Your shift moves letters along twenty-six.

other_ways.note: translate() swaps every letter at once, using a table from the alphabet to the shifted alphabet.
The same steps in one line with join(); encode() uses UTF-8 when no encoding is named.
